clue.text: Suffering from gout? Not half, some will admit

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so one word takes the other inside it

parts.note: some and any are interchangeable determiners, as in 'have you any?'

indicators.note: only half of the word is kept, so the other half is dropped

parts.note: taken as written, then cut to its first half

explanation.surface: A gout sufferer admits only to some of the pain, playing it down.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pairs suffering with gout, but gout is fodder; only its first half is used, held inside the word for some.
explanation.definitionFit: Agony is extreme pain, so it is a stronger synonym for suffering as a noun.

clue.text: Cheers Bill, overcoming allegations

indicators.note: in a down answer, coming over means sitting on top, so the bill word goes first

parts.note: AC is short for account, a bill
claims are allegations, assertions not yet proven

explanation.surface: A man named Bill gets a cheer after clearing his name of accusations.
explanation.walkthrough: Bill looks like a name, but it is an account, AC.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheers as a verb means applauds, and acclaims means praises enthusiastically and publicly.

clue.text: Contemporary delays treatment, essentially relating to sight

indicators.note: delaying something puts it later in line, so the letter is lifted out and set further along

parts.note: topical means of current interest, contemporary

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its core, so only its central letter is taken

parts.note: the middle letter of treatment

explanation.surface: Modern methods slow down an eye treatment, which essentially concerns vision.
explanation.walkthrough: TOPICAL's opening T, the core of treatment, is moved two places later to give OP-T-ICAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Optical is the adjective for anything concerning vision or the eye.

clue.text: Measures succeeded to intercept garden parasites

indicators.note: to intercept is to get in the way between, so the letter lands inside the phrase

parts.note: a yard is a garden, especially in American usage
S is the abbreviation for succeeded, as in family trees
ticks are blood-sucking parasites

explanation.surface: Steps taken to stop pests getting into the garden worked.
explanation.definitionFit: A yardstick is a standard used for comparison, so yardsticks are measures.

clue.text: Mentions bands appearing in tavern, making comeback

indicators.note: showing up inside somewhere puts one word within the other
a comeback runs back the way it came, so the tavern word is read backwards

parts.note: a pub is a tavern
rings are circular bands

explanation.surface: Musical groups are playing a pub again after some time away.
explanation.walkthrough: Bands suggests musicians playing a pub, but here they are circular rings.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring up a topic is to raise it in conversation, the same as mentioning it.

clue.text: Typical ambassador, say

definitions.meaning: first meaning: characteristic of a class, as an adjective
second meaning: someone who acts for another; say flags an ambassador as one example

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as 'a typical ambassador', but the words are two separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both characteristic of a group and, as a noun, a person who speaks or acts for others, like a diplomat.

clue.text: Element in news once, repeatedly seen half-cut

indicators.note: each of the two words is cut in half, so the back halves are dropped

parts.note: taken as written, then halved
taken as written, then halved

explanation.surface: Someone who once kept appearing drunk in the news headlines.
explanation.walkthrough: Half-cut is British slang for drunk; here it just means the two words lose half their letters each.
explanation.definitionFit: Neon is a chemical element, the inert gas used in glowing signs.

clue.text: Extra menu item selected at first, battered plaice

indicators.note: at first points to the opening letter only

parts.note: the first letter of selected

indicators.note: battered means knocked about, so the letters are beaten out of shape

parts.note: the fish, taken as written to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A restaurant's dish of the day is battered plaice.
explanation.walkthrough: Battered fits fried fish perfectly, which hides its job as the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A special is a dish offered in addition to the usual menu, often for one day only.

clue.text: To his friends television interviewer is cold

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the nickname of Sir Michael Parkinson, the British chat-show host
second meaning: British slang for chilly weather

explanation.walkthrough: Michael Parkinson hosted the long-running BBC chat show Parkinson; parky is also informal British for cold.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is Parkinson's familiar nickname and also a colloquial British adjective for chilly.

clue.text: Medicine almost cured a Tamil chap, surprisingly

indicators.note: a surprising result comes out in an unexpected form, so the letters are rearranged
almost means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written, then shortened
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A drug has nearly cured a Tamil man, to everyone's surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: A pharmaceutical is a medicinal drug, the noun use of the adjective.

clue.text: Airways reportedly showing build-up of mucus

indicators.note: what is reported is heard rather than read, so go by the sound

parts.note: Airways suggests Qatar Airways, the Gulf state's airline; the country's name is said much like the medical word

explanation.surface: An airline's report reveals a problem in passengers' breathing passages.
explanation.walkthrough: Airways looks like the respiratory tract, fitting mucus, but it stands for the airline of Qatar.
explanation.definitionFit: Catarrh is the medical term for excess mucus collecting in the nose and throat.

clue.text: Support inspiring individual, innovator

indicators.note: inspiring literally means breathing in, so one word draws the other inside

parts.note: a pier is a supporting pillar or column
one is a single individual

explanation.surface: Backing an inspiring person who comes up with new ideas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inspiring individual' reads as a phrase praising someone; split it, and inspiring is the instruction to put one word inside the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A pioneer is the first to develop a new method or area, which makes them an innovator.

clue.text: Origins of cases of arson crime son hears

indicators.note: a case is the outside shell, so only the outer letters of the next two words are used

parts.note: first and last letters of arson
first and last letters of crime
S is the standard abbreviation for son
a judge hears or tries a case in court

explanation.surface: A judge hears where several arson cases began, and one involves a son.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cases of' does double duty over arson and crime; the courtroom surface makes hears fit the judge who tries.
explanation.definitionFit: Your ancestries are your lines of descent, the family origins you come from.

clue.text: Maybe London detective on screen's lacking in truthfulness?

indicators.note: something lacking in a word has been taken out of it, so remove the first piece from the second

parts.note: veracity means truthfulness
Vera is the TV detective DCI Vera Stanhope of the ITV series Vera

explanation.surface: A TV detective in London turns out to be not very honest.
explanation.walkthrough: Vera is a long-running British crime drama. Take VERA from VERACITY and the rest is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: London is an example of a city, which 'Maybe' signals as definition by example.

clue.text: Good person taking over shortly African politicians protected

indicators.note: taking in means holding within, so the good person surrounds the rest

parts.note: ST is short for saint, a good person

indicators.note: shortly means in brief, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: across means over, from one side to the other
the ANC is the African National Congress, South Africa's governing party

explanation.surface: A saintly figure briefly takes charge, and African politicians are kept safe.
explanation.definitionFit: Sacrosanct means too important to be interfered with, so protected from criticism or change.

clue.text: Last month I departed after mass gathering involving many groups

indicators.note: after places the first run of words behind the next one in the answer

parts.note: M is the physics symbol for mass
ult., short for ultimo, means of last month in old business letters
taken as written
the late someone is someone who has died, or departed
a rally is a mass gathering of people

explanation.surface: Someone recalls leaving after a big church service and a meeting last month.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mass' reads as a church service, but it is the physics symbol. Ult., for ultimo, is old commercial shorthand for last month.
explanation.definitionFit: Multilaterally describes action taken by several parties or nations together, involving many groups at once.

clue.text: Man's found here in plant as he works

parts.note: the iris is a flowering plant

indicators.note: works means operates or is worked on, so these letters are set to work in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A man is found at the factory, at work among the machinery.
explanation.walkthrough: Man is not a person but the Isle of Man, which lies in the stretch of sea between Britain and Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isle of Man sits in the Irish Sea, so that is where Man is found.

clue.text: Annoying car passenger favours snack approaching golf club

parts.note: to back a side is to favour it
to snack is to eat, as a verb
a driver is the golf club used for long tee shots

explanation.surface: An irritating passenger who prefers eating on the way to the golf club.
explanation.walkthrough: Snack is a verb here, to eat; favours is a verb too, to back.
explanation.definitionFit: A back-seat driver is a passenger who keeps giving the driver unwanted advice, which is annoying.

clue.text: Not all loathe artificiality basically

indicators.note: only part of the following words is used, so the letters run inside them

parts.note: the end of loathe and the start of artificiality

explanation.surface: Not everyone hates pretence, when you get down to it.
explanation.definitionFit: At heart means in one's fundamental nature, which is what basically means.

clue.text: Fabian regularly wears American waistcoat, getting most conceited

indicators.note: what you wear goes round you, so the waistcoat surrounds the kept letters

parts.note: vest is the American word for a waistcoat

indicators.note: at regular intervals means every other letter is taken

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: Fabian often wears an American-style waistcoat, becoming ever more vain.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a vest is an undershirt; the American sense, a waistcoat, is the one needed.
explanation.definitionFit: Vainest is the superlative of vain, meaning having the highest opinion of oneself.

clue.text: Repeat extract from speech obsessively

indicators.note: an extract is a piece taken from inside a longer passage, so the letters sit within the words that follow

parts.note: the end of speech and the start of obsessively

explanation.surface: Someone keeps quoting part of a speech over and over.
explanation.definitionFit: To echo is to repeat what someone else has said, as a sound repeats off a wall.

clue.text: Old comic with dog, removing its lead

indicators.note: a lead goes in front, so the first letter is taken away

parts.note: a beagle is a breed of hound

explanation.surface: An elderly comedian with a dog lets it off the leash.
explanation.walkthrough: Comic is the magazine, not a comedian: The Eagle was a British boys' comic of the 1950s and 60s, home of Dan Dare.
explanation.definitionFit: The Eagle was a famous weekly British children's comic paper, now long closed.

clue.text: Branch of maths, still claiming it's scrambled student's head

indicators.note: to claim something is to take hold of it, so one word holds the other

parts.note: static means still, not moving

indicators.note: scrambled letters are mixed up and reordered

parts.note: taken as written, without the apostrophe

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: the first letter of student

explanation.surface: A student's brain is muddled by mathematics, and still claims it.
explanation.walkthrough: STATIC holds a mixed-up ITS, then the S from student finishes it.
explanation.definitionFit: Statistics is the branch of mathematics dealing with collecting and analysing numerical data.

clue.text: Cut broadcast for US showbiz legend

indicators.note: a broadcast is heard over the air, so go by the sound of the word

parts.note: to shear is to cut, and the singer's name is said the same way

explanation.surface: A TV programme was cut short for an American celebrity.
explanation.definitionFit: Cher is the American singer and actress whose career has spanned six decades.

clue.text: Explicit illustration

definitions.meaning: first meaning: shown in vivid, often shocking detail
second meaning: a picture or diagram, as a noun

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a description of a racy picture, but the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Graphic works as an adjective for vividly detailed content and as a noun for a visual image or diagram.

clue.text: Archdeacon is briefed occasionally about cosmetic dental options

parts.note: an archdeacon is styled the Venerable, abbreviated Ven

indicators.note: about can mean turned round, so the kept letters are read backwards
occasionally means now and then, so only every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: A senior cleric gets an occasional briefing on having his teeth whitened.
explanation.walkthrough: Ven. is the title used for an Anglican archdeacon, the Venerable.
explanation.definitionFit: Veneers are thin shells bonded to the front of teeth to improve their look, a cosmetic dental treatment.

clue.text: Bank on legume being peeled? Quite

indicators.note: on means placed after, so the bank word comes second
peeling takes off the outer skin, so the first and last letters go

parts.note: the lentil is a legume
to bank on something is to rely on it

explanation.surface: A cook wonders whether to count on a peeled bean, then agrees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank on' looks like one phrase, but on is the positional word placing the bank piece after the peeled legume.
explanation.definitionFit: Quite in the sense of completely or wholly means the same as entirely.

clue.text: Tense period maintaining temperature for tropical fish

parts.note: T is the grammar abbreviation for tense

indicators.note: to maintain is to hold or keep, so one word holds the other within

parts.note: an era is a period of time
T is the symbol for temperature

explanation.surface: A nervous spell spent keeping the water warm enough for tropical fish.
explanation.walkthrough: ERA keeps the temperature T inside after its E, and the T for tense goes in front.
explanation.definitionFit: A tetra is a small, often brightly coloured freshwater fish from tropical rivers, popular in aquariums.
